name: Babyface vs mature face

lead: Babyfaceness describes faces that resemble infants: larger eyes, a smaller nose and chin, a rounder face and softer contours. Mature faces have the opposite cues, with more angular structure. Psychologists find that people read babyfaced adults as warmer and more naive, and mature faces as more dominant.

Looksmaxxers use the contrast to decide what to change, for example leaning out to reveal structure or keeping youthful features. Many respond that babyface can also be attractive; the research on first impressions is extensive.

paras: In practice people discuss body fat, facial lean-ness, jaw and eye-area structure, grooming such as facial hair, and hairstyle as the levers that shift a face toward youthful or mature. Forum threads ask what causes a babyface and how to "fix" it, with answers ranging from bloat to bone structure.

The idea itself is descriptive. Community claims about hormones or growth hormone changing the face to look more mature are not backed by research on the framework, and growth hormone excess (acromegaly) is a medical condition.

angle.text: The framework tells people which features drive impressions of youth or maturity, so they can choose changes such as leanness or facial hair that shift the read.

lead: Babyface versus mature face contrasts two ends of a perceptual dimension. Babyfaced people have features resembling infants, such as large eyes, a small jaw and a rounded face, while mature faces show more angular, developed structure.[1][2]

Konrad Lorenz proposed in 1949 that infantile features, which he called the baby schema, evolved to prompt caretaking: a large forehead and eyes, small nose, mouth and jaw, and round cheeks.[3] Psychologists extend this as the babyface overgeneralization effect, in which adults who resemble babies are judged as more naive, warm and trusting.[1][2][4]

In looksmaxxing forums the contrast is a recurring topic: one thread called babyface an undertalked problem, while another argues it is not a death sentence, citing Perrett's work on attractiveness.[5][6] How a face reads is a core question for anyone changing their look.
infobox: Large eyes, small jaw/chin, round face

paras: Researchers describe a baby schema of cues including a larger head and forehead, larger eyes, a smaller nose, mouth and chin, and rounded cheeks.[3] Studies of adult responses show neutral infant expressions give the strongest baby-schema effect.[7]

The overgeneralization hypothesis holds that responses suited to babies spill over to adults with similar structure. Neuroimaging has found amygdala and fusiform face area activation to babyfaced men that matches activation to babies.[1] Reviews of face perception describe babyface cues as one of several qualities, with low-fitness, emotion and identity cues, that drive impressions.[2]

Experimental work has found that emotion expressions resembling babies or adults shape trait impressions.[8] Cross-cultural comparisons of Chinese and American participants tested whether babyfaced people are seen as naive, cute and trustworthy.[9] Studies with older and younger adults found babyface stereotypes and the attractiveness halo effect in both groups.[4] An attention study found female babyfaces and male mature faces held gaze longer.[10]

On looksmax.org, one thread asks what causes a babyface and how to fix it, with replies naming bloat or an eye area and jaw structure.[5] Another thread argues babyface can be attractive and quotes work on how faces enhanced in masculinity were described as cold; a reply there links babyface to "low T, high E".[6] A third thread discusses growth hormone excess in a famous public figure as a route from boyish to mature features, and replies debate it.[11]
No clinical studies found on changing babyface or mature features. Psychology experiments on perception of babyfaceness are described above.[8][7][1]
